1.source: Stroll the bricks of Church Street
1.title: Stroll the bricks of Church Street
1.paragraph: Start at the top of the bricks and let the Church Street Marketplace set the pace, four pedestrian blocks with street entertainers, cart vendors and over 100 shops and restaurants. Duck into Outdoor Gear Exchange at 37 Church Street and head down to the consignment desk in the basement, where used gear gets a second life. Then browse Flora & Fauna at 70 Church Street for taxidermy, fossils and oddities. Finish with a scoop at Ben & Jerry's at 36 Church Street, a fitting last stop, since Ben and Jerry opened their very first shop in 1978 in a renovated gas station on St. Paul Street, across from City Hall Park.

notes.church-street-marketplace: Four pedestrian blocks since 1981, with buskers and over 100 businesses
notes.outdoor-gear-exchange: The consignment desk in the basement is where the used gear deals live
notes.flora-and-fauna: Taxidermy, fossils and oddities at 70 Church Street, woman owned
notes.ben-jerrys-church-street: The scoop shop for a company that began in a St. Paul Street gas station

2.source: Watch the sun drop behind the Adirondacks
2.title: Watch the sun drop behind the Adirondacks
2.paragraph: Check the sky before dinner, and if the clouds look promising, pick your spot. Try for one of the swinging benches on the Waterfront Park boardwalk for the view at water level, or climb up to Battery Park for the wide look over the lake toward the Adirondacks, from the same high point where cannons turned back a British attack in 1813. For something quieter, walk out to the last strip of grass at Lakeview Cemetery, the Victorian park cemetery on North Avenue. Or head to the South End and stand inside the Earth Clock at Oakledge Park, 14 granite stones that track where the sun meets the horizon through the seasons.

notes.waterfront-park: Water level on the boardwalk, if you can claim one of the swinging benches
notes.battery-park: The high view over the lake to the Adirondacks, named for the cannons of 1813
notes.lakeview-cemetery: A quiet Victorian park cemetery with a strip of grass above the lake
notes.earth-clock-oakledge: Fourteen granite stones at Oakledge that track the sun along the horizon

3.source: Bike the causeway out into the middle of the lake
3.title: Bike the causeway out into the middle of the lake
3.paragraph: Reserve a bike at Local Motion's Trailside Center at 1 Steele Street, then ride north on the Island Line Trail. The pavement turns to crushed gravel at Airport Park, and soon you're out on the Colchester Causeway, built of Rutland marble for the 1899 Island Line Railroad, with the Adirondacks and Green Mountains in view. It's windier out there than the forecast admits and there's barely any shade, so bring a jacket and water. At the Cut, the bike ferry carries you across for a suggested $5 donation. On a summer Thursday, roll on to Snow Farm Vineyard in South Hero for the free concert on the lawn, then ride back the way you came.

notes.island-line-causeway: A three mile marble causeway built for the 1899 railroad, now a bike trail
notes.local-motion: Rents bikes and e-bikes on the trail and runs the ferry across the Cut
notes.snow-farm-vineyard: The South Hero payoff, with free Thursday concerts all summer

4.source: Eat a maple creemee, then settle the argument
4.title: Eat a maple creemee, then settle the argument
4.paragraph: Start on the waterfront with a maple creemee from Burlington Bay Market & Café at 125 Battery Street, where it's the best seller, or from Champ's Legendary Creemees, the ECHO stand that runs May through early October with all proceeds going to the museum. Then drive out to Palmer Lane Maple at 19 Old Pump Road in Jericho and order the Maple Sundae, a small maple creemee drizzled with pure Vermont syrup and topped with real maple sprinkles. Finish at the Village Scoop, attached to the original Colchester schoolhouse, and try the Tornado, the local special. By then you'll have your own answer to the question of who does it best.

notes.burlington-bay-creemee: The waterfront window where maple is the best selling creemee
notes.champs-creemees: ECHO's own stand, May to early October, with proceeds to the museum
notes.palmer-lane-maple: Real maple sprinkles and pure syrup on a Jericho maple sundae
notes.village-scoop: Colchester's drive-through classic, home of the Tornado

5.title: Crawl the South End's taprooms
5.paragraph: Start at Zero Gravity's beer hall at 716 Pine Street with a Conehead IPA or a crisp Green State Lager out on the sunny outdoor seating. Walk down to Queen City Brewery at 703 Pine Street, pull up to the 50 year old mahogany bar and be brave with the Rauchbier, made in the Bamberg tradition with malt smoked over beech wood. Then head over to Flynn Avenue. Citizen Cider's Press House Pub at 180 Flynn Avenue offers free tastings in its store and food in the pub, and Switchback at 160 Flynn Avenue closes out the crawl with house-smoked BBQ in its Beer Garden & Smokehouse.

notes.zero-gravity-brewery: The beer hall for the Citra Conehead IPA and the Green State Lager
notes.queen-city-brewery: Old world styles and a smoked Rauchbier at a 50 year old mahogany bar
notes.citizen-cider: Cider pressed in Burlington, free tastings and a family friendly pub
notes.switchback-brewing: 100% employee owned, with house smoked BBQ in the beer garden

6.source: Drink a beer by the lake at golden hour
6.title: Drink a beer by the lake at golden hour
6.paragraph: Get to Foam Brewers at 112 Lake Street while the sun is still up, grab a spot on the patio, which has its own bar in the warmer months, and order the Tranquil Pils, a crisp German pilsner, with some cheese and charcuterie. The view runs west over Lake Champlain to the Adirondack Mountains, so you can watch the light change without moving. If you want to talk beer, come on a weekday, when the staff has more time and the brewhouse sits in plain sight of the bar. The draft list rotates, so ask what just went on.

notes.foam-brewers: A westward view over the lake, a patio bar and a rotating draft list

7.source: Shop the farmers markets, Saturday and Tuesday
7.title: Shop the farmers markets, Saturday and Tuesday
7.paragraph: Take the #5 bus, which stops at the market every half hour on Saturdays, or bike over and lock up at the racks, then spend the morning at the Burlington Farmers Market at 345 Pine Street, open 9 to 2. Walk the rows of farmers, specialty food producers and artisan crafts, and eat as you go. On Tuesday afternoon, head to Dewey Park, where Archibald, Spring and Walnut Streets meet, for the Old North End Farmers Market from 3 to 6:30. Grab a loaf of Tremolo bread, baked in a stone oven just before the market, and pick up dinner from Kalaat Moroccan Kitchen or Yalla Eats.

notes.burlington-farmers-market: Saturdays on Pine Street since 1980, 9 to 2, May through October
notes.one-farmers-market: Tuesday afternoons in Dewey Park, with Moroccan and Yemeni cooking

8.source: Lose a full day at Shelburne Museum
8.title: Lose a full day at Shelburne Museum
8.paragraph: Get there when the gates open at 10, anytime from May into late October, and start with the Ticonderoga, the 220 foot steamboat sitting on the grounds. From there wander through the lighthouse, the jail and the Shaker design Round Barn, ride the 1920s carousel, and save time for Webb Gallery, where Andrew Wyeth and Winslow Homer hang. Your ticket is good for two consecutive days, so there's no need to see all 39 buildings at once, and Vermont residents pay $15 at the door. Come back in late November for Winter Lights, when the grounds glitter after dark.

notes.shelburne-museum: 39 buildings on 45 acres, from a lighthouse to the steamboat Ticonderoga

9.source: Walk the Vanderbilt estate at Shelburne Farms
9.title: Walk the Vanderbilt estate at Shelburne Farms
9.paragraph: From mid-May to mid-October, check in at the Farm Store at 1611 Harbor Road, the old North Gatehouse of the Webb estate, and grab a trail map. Walk the trail out to the Farm Barn, or hop the shuttle wagon, and watch the cheesemakers turn Brown Swiss milk into cheddar, then try a sample, while the kids meet the animals at the Children's Farmyard. Spend the afternoon on the more than 10 miles of trails through fields and forest. If you booked ahead, finish with dinner at the Inn, which serves the farm's own cheese, meats and produce. The rest of the year, the store and trails stay open.

notes.shelburne-farms: Cheddar from Brown Swiss milk and 10 miles of trails, by donation

10.source: Meet the lake's residents at ECHO
10.title: Meet the lake's residents at ECHO
10.paragraph: Time your visit to ECHO at 1 College Street around the 11 or 2 o'clock animal presentation, when the care team brings out creatures like American eels, snapping turtles and Eastern newts. Then work your way through all three levels, hunting for the lake sturgeon, the longnosed gar and the mudpuppy among more than 50 native species. Save the Champ exhibit for last, where you can weigh the 1977 Mansi photo, learn about P.T. Barnum's 1873 reward and stand next to a sculpture over 30 feet long. It's open daily, year round, which makes it the waterfront's answer to a rainy afternoon.

notes.echo-leahy-center: Over 50 native lake species and a 30 foot Champ, open year round

11.source: Pick a city beach and get in the lake
11.title: Pick a city beach and get in the lake
11.paragraph: Decide what kind of beach day you're after. For the full setup, go to North Beach off Institute Road, the largest of the bunch, with a concession stand, showers and summer kayak and paddleboard rentals, and plan on $3 an hour for parking from May to mid-October. For room to spread out, Leddy Beach has 1,500 feet of sand, grills on the grassy picnic area and free parking. If the dog is coming, Texaco Beach is the city's only dedicated dog beach, reached off the Greenway. For a quieter swim, take the bike path to Oakledge Cove, the most secluded of the five, and stay for sunset on the rocks.

notes.north-beach: The largest, with concessions, showers and summer paddle rentals
notes.leddy-beach: A 1,500 foot sandy beach with grills and free parking, no lifeguard
notes.texaco-beach: The city's only dedicated dog beach, open to dogs year round
notes.oakledge-park: The Cove is the most secluded beach, with rocks and quiet sunsets

12.source: Ride the Greenway end to end
12.title: Ride the Greenway end to end
12.paragraph: Rent a bike or e-bike at Local Motion's Trailside Center at 1 Steele Street, grab a free helmet and borrow a lock, then point yourself south to the start just before Oakledge Park. Turn around and ride the whole eight miles north past the parks and the waterfront to the pedestrian bridge over the Winooski River, stopping wherever looks good. Ride single file, give people on foot the right of way and say "passing on your left" with a ring of the bell. Full day rentals come back by 6. In winter, bring skis instead, since the city plows the lake side and leaves the east side for skiing.

notes.burlington-greenway: Eight paved miles on the lake, plowed in winter with a side left to ski
notes.local-motion: Bikes, e-bikes, trailers and adaptive bikes right on the path

13.source: Walk out to the Champlain Thrust Fault at Rock Point
13.title: Walk out to the Champlain Thrust Fault at Rock Point
13.paragraph: Request the free digital trail pass online, then park at Leddy Park and walk south on the bike path about half a mile to the Holy Trinity Trail trailhead, the approach Rock Point itself recommends. Follow the trails out to Lone Rock Point, where the Champlain Thrust Fault is exposed, older Cambrian dolostone resting on dark gray Ordovician shale streaked with white calcite. Stay on the trails, since this is one of the most significant rare plant sites in Vermont, keep the dog leashed and leave the bike at the racks. In winter, wear microspikes near the 60 foot cliff edges, where the trail gets icy.

notes.rock-point: One of North America's most visible thrust fault exposures, free with a pass

14.source: See a show at the Flynn
14.title: See a show at the Flynn
14.paragraph: Pick a show from the Flynn's calendar, which runs to more than 200 performances a year, and get to 153 Main Street early enough to look around. The 1,439 seat Main Stage has welcomed audiences since 1930 and was restored in its original Art Deco style, so take in the room, then stop by the Amy E. Tarrant Gallery off the lobby, which rotates work by regional artists. For something smaller, Flynn Space seats about 200 for theater, music, comedy and experimental performance. Come June, the Flynn's Burlington Discover Jazz Festival brings local, national and international artists to venues and public spaces.

notes.flynn-center: A 1930 Art Deco house with 1,439 seats and the Discover Jazz Festival

15.source: Hear live music downtown, from jazz jam to dance floor
15.title: Hear live music downtown, from jazz jam to dance floor
15.paragraph: Start on College Street at The 126, a 21 and over cocktail room with a weekly music lineup. Tuesday is Big Easy Tuesdays with Jon McBride, Wednesday is the jazz jam with the house band, where musicians of any level can sit in, and Thursday brings Alex Stewart's quartet followed by a funk jam. Fridays and Saturdays have jazz sets at 7 or 9. When the set ends, walk over to Red Square at 136 Church Street, open Thursday through Saturday, where live bands and DJs keep the crowd on its feet.

notes.deli-126: Weekly jazz and funk jams plus weekend jazz sets on College Street
notes.red-square: Live bands and DJs on Church Street, Thursday through Saturday

16.source: Book one of downtown's big dinners
16.title: Book one of downtown's big dinners
16.paragraph: Pick your table a few days ahead. For daily changing Vermont cooking, book Hen of the Wood beside Hotel Vermont and look for the Hen of the Woods Mushroom Toast. For a group that likes to share, Honey Road on Church Street lays out Eastern Mediterranean mezze, so start with house made pita, the dips and the Lamb Cracker. A Single Pebble on Bank Street serves family style Wednesday through Saturday, and the Mock Eel should be the first thing you order. For something classic, Leunig's Bistro at Church and College does a $28 two course early bird, with some of the best people watching downtown.

notes.hen-of-the-wood: Daily changing Vermont menu beside Hotel Vermont, mushroom toast on it
notes.honey-road: Eastern Mediterranean mezze from four time James Beard finalist Cara Tobin
notes.a-single-pebble: Family style Chinese on Bank Street, with crispy shiitake mock eel
notes.leunigs-bistro: The French bistro at Church and College, with a $28 early bird

17.source: Climb Mt. Philo, then eat at Philo Ridge Farm
17.title: Climb Mt. Philo, then eat at Philo Ridge Farm
17.paragraph: Park at the bottom of Mt. Philo State Park, pay the $5 day use fee and hike the three quarter mile trail to the 968 foot summit, or drive the summit road if hiking isn't the plan. In fall, bring binoculars, since the park is noted for raptor watching and autumn migrations, and take in the Lake Champlain Valley out to the Adirondack Mountains. Then head to Philo Ridge Farm at 2766 Mount Philo Road. Walk in for lunch Wednesday through Saturday, made from what the farm grows and raises, then browse the Market for its own produce and grass-fed meats before you drive home.

notes.mt-philo-state-park: Vermont's first state park, a 968 foot summit you can hike or drive
notes.philo-ridge-farm: Walk-in lunch and a market fed by the farm's own 500 acres

18.source: Earn the summit of Camel's Hump
18.title: Earn the summit of Camel's Hump
18.paragraph: Get to the Burrows Trail lot at the end of Camel's Hump Road in Huntington by about 8 on a nice weekend, since the lot fills and cars parked along the road get towed. Climb Burrows, pick up the Long Trail south and follow it to the summit for 360 degree views. Stay on the marked trail up top, because this is one of only three Vermont summits with rare arctic alpine plants. Carry a paper map and check the mountain forecast first, as the Green Mountain Club advises. Trails close in mud season and reopen the weekend before Memorial Day.

notes.camels-hump: A free 4,083 foot summit with rare alpine plants on the Long Trail

19.source: Get to the top of Mount Mansfield, any way you like
19.title: Get to the top of Mount Mansfield, any way you like
19.paragraph: For the classic climb, carpool to Underhill State Park, pay the $5 day use fee and take the Sunset Ridge Trail, a 3 mile route up the west side to the Long Trail and north to the Chin, Vermont's highest point at 4,395 feet. On the ridge, stay on the marked trail, since the alpine plants up there are rare and fragile. If your legs aren't up for it, ride the Stowe gondola and hike the Cliff House Trail, or drive the Stowe Toll Road to the ridgeline. Underhill's season runs from Memorial Day weekend to the second Monday in October.

notes.mount-mansfield: Vermont's high point, with the largest alpine zone and 28 trails
notes.underhill-state-park: The west side start for Sunset Ridge, with a CCC-built pavilion

20.source: Get out on the lake by sailboat or cruise boat
20.title: Get out on the lake by sailboat or cruise boat
20.paragraph: For the quiet version, book a shared sail with Whistling Man Schooner Co. from slips 35 and 36 at the Burlington Community Boathouse, pack a picnic and a bottle, since it's BYO, and bring a layer, because it's usually cooler on the water than on shore. A licensed captain and deckhand handle the sailing for two hours, so nobody needs to know how. For the party version, board the Spirit of Ethan Allen at 1 College Street for a narrated scenic cruise or the nightly sunset cruise, with DJs on summer Fridays and Saturdays. Both run from spring into October, so book ahead.

notes.whistling-man-schooner: Two hour BYO sails on classic sloops, six to ten guests, from $68
notes.spirit-of-ethan-allen: The big boat, with narrated scenic cruises and nightly sunset runs

21.source: Eat dinner practically in the lake
21.title: Eat dinner practically in the lake
21.paragraph: Start with a drink at Splash at the Boathouse, where the tables sit right on the docks of the Burlington Boathouse and the kitchen turns out tacos, wraps and burgers from 11 until sunset. Walk down to Spot on the Dock at 1 King Street for coconut shrimp or a lobster roll, and grab a seat in the lounge if there's a wait, since they don't take reservations. For something more old school, Shanty on the Shore at 181 Battery Street has served seafood under its original wood beams since 1985, with specials that change daily. Come back the next morning for crepes at The Skinny Pancake.

notes.splash-boathouse: Tacos and a full bar right on the Boathouse docks, open until sunset
notes.spot-on-the-dock: Surf shack energy and lobster rolls at 1 King Street, mid May to late September
notes.shanty-on-shore: Seafood in an 1833 waterfront building, the Shanty since 1985
notes.skinny-pancake: Crepes by the lake from 7:30 every morning, beer and cocktails later

22.source: Make a night of comedy and games
22.title: Make a night of comedy and games
22.paragraph: Start early at The Boardroom, the board game cafe at 3 Mill Street, where $6 a person gets you the run of more than 700 games and the staff will teach you one you've never played. Order a bucket of Bugles and stay until showtime. Then head to Vermont Comedy Club at 101 Main Street, where Wednesday brings the $5 improv night at 6:30 and a free open mic at 8:30, and Thursday through Saturday bring the touring headliners. Finish at The Archives on College Street, an arcade bar with 24 taps, Pac-Man, NBA Jam and pinball machines.

notes.boardroom-games: Over 700 games for $6 a person, with staff who teach you the rules
notes.vermont-comedy-club: A 140 seat room with touring headliners and a free Wednesday open mic
notes.archives-bar: Vintage arcade cabinets and pinball with 24 rotating taps on College Street

23.source: Catch a touring act at Higher Ground
23.title: Catch a touring act at Higher Ground
23.paragraph: Pull up the calendar first, because Higher Ground produces over 300 shows a year and something is almost always on. The club sits at 1214 Williston Road in South Burlington, where it landed after starting out in Winooski back in 1998. Grab dinner nearby, then head in and catch whoever is passing through. This is the outfit that has backed Noah Kahan, Anais Mitchell, Grace Potter and Phish, so the fun is catching the next name on the way up. Watch the same calendar for their shows at Waterfront Park and Shelburne Museum too.

notes.higher-ground: Over 300 shows a year on Williston Road, at it since 1998

24.source: Watch the sap boil at a Vermont sugarhouse
24.title: Watch the sap boil at a Vermont sugarhouse
24.paragraph: Plan it for March, when the steam is rising. In Shelburne, Palmer's Sugarhouse runs maple demonstrations and free samples in sugaring season and serves traditional sugar on snow. For a full day, drive to Montpelier and up to Morse Farm, where the sugarhouse is open to the public in season, the Woodshed Theatre plays a video on sugarmaking, and sugar on snow comes with a donut and a pickle. Finish at Bragg Farm in East Montpelier for a free sugarhouse tour and a maple creemee. Better yet, aim for Maple Open House Weekend, March 20 and 21, 2027.

notes.palmers-sugarhouse: Shelburne's family sugarhouse, demonstrations and sugar on snow each March
notes.morse-farm-maple: Hilltop sugarworks with a sugar wood theatre and sugar on snow with a pickle
notes.bragg-farm: Buckets, a wood fired evaporator, free sugarhouse tours, creemees year round

25.source: Eat breakfast at a classic diner
25.title: Eat breakfast at a classic diner
25.paragraph: Pick your counter. Downtown, Henry's Diner at 155 Bank Street has been feeding Burlington since 1925, and the homemade corned beef hash with two eggs is the classic order. Over on Maple Street, Handy's Lunch has run since 1945 with the third generation of Handys on the grill, and the brave can try the Chuck Norris, five slices of French toast stacked with four eggs, bacon, ham, sausage, a burger and corned beef. If you'd rather drive, the Parkway Diner on Williston Road serves its famous French toast in an original 1950s dining car, with biscuits made in house.

notes.henrys-diner: Bank Street's railroad dining car since 1925, homemade corned beef hash
notes.handy-lunch: A horseshoe counter, third generation Handys, and the Chuck Norris
notes.parkway-diner: An original 1950s dining car on Williston Road, biscuits made in house

26.source: Walk the rocky shoreline at Red Rocks Park
26.title: Walk the rocky shoreline at Red Rocks Park
26.paragraph: Park off Central Avenue in South Burlington and take the trails into the hemlock and pine, where the loops wind out onto a rocky shoreline over Shelburne Bay. Find a spot on the rocks and look across Lake Champlain to the Adirondacks. On a hot day, follow the paths down to the beach, which is open to the public without lifeguards, and check the posted water results, since the city tests for E. coli every Monday and Wednesday in season. Bikes stay off the foot trails. Come back in winter, when the same 100 acres take snowshoes and cross country skis.

notes.red-rocks-park: Wooded loops that end on a rocky shoreline over Shelburne Bay

27.source: Climb the treehouse at Oakledge Park
27.title: Climb the treehouse at Oakledge Park
27.paragraph: Come in at the west end of Flynn Avenue, or ride the Burlington Greenway straight into the park. Head first for the treehouse, a 500 square foot platform built in 2004 up in a red oak, reached by a wooden pier so a wheelchair can roll right in. From there, wander down to one of the two beaches or out along the rocky lakeside cliffs. Kids can take over the playground, which has universal access features, while everyone else claims a bocce court. Save time for the Upper and Lower Wetland at the south end, which offer places to watch birds.

notes.oakledge-park: A 2004 treehouse in a red oak built for wheelchairs, plus two beaches

28.source: Walk under the girders of the Moran Frame
28.title: Walk under the girders of the Moran Frame
28.paragraph: Walk north along the waterfront until the red steel comes into view. That frame was the Moran Municipal Generating Station, a coal plant that opened in 1954 and was decommissioned in 1986, and the city stripped its brick in 2022 and 2023 so you can wander under the girders with Lake Champlain right there. Find the two swinging benches hung in the northwest bay and take a turn. Check what Friends of the FRAME has scheduled, since the group puts on free events there. Then stay until the light goes gold on the steel.

notes.moran-frame: A 1954 coal plant stripped to its red steel frame, free to walk under

29.source: Wander the halls of the old Soda Plant
29.title: Wander the halls of the old Soda Plant
29.paragraph: Start with a coffee at Brio Coffeeworks, the roastery and coffee bar inside the Soda Plant at 266 Pine Street, where Venetian ginger ale was first bottled back in 1917. Walk the cup over to the S.P.A.C.E. Gallery, open Thursday through Saturday from 12 to 5, and see what's on the walls this month. If it's the First Friday of the month, come back for the evening reception. Close the day at Venetian Soda Lounge, a 48 seat speakeasy in the same building, with a $5 ginger ale or a cocktail while a jazz or blues act plays.

notes.soda-plant: The 1917 ginger ale bottling plant, now studios, shops and a gallery
notes.brio-coffeeworks: A woman owned roaster with its coffee bar right in the building
notes.venetian-soda-lounge: A 48 seat speakeasy pouring $5 house sodas and live jazz most nights

30.source: Hop between galleries on Church Street
30.title: Hop between galleries on Church Street
30.paragraph: Start at the BCA Center, 135 Church Street, where Burlington City Arts fills three levels with rotating exhibitions. It opens at noon Wednesday through Saturday and stays open until 8 on Wednesdays and Saturdays, so an evening visit is easy. Then walk down the bricks to Frog Hollow at 85 Church Street, the craft gallery that became the first state craft center in the nation in 1975. Browse work from over 100 Vermont artists and pick out something small to take home.

notes.bca-center: Burlington City Arts' three level exhibition space, open until 8 Wed and Sat
notes.frog-hollow-gallery: The first state craft center in the nation, with over 100 Vermont artists

31.source: Cheer on a home team on a summer night
31.title: Cheer on a home team on a summer night
31.paragraph: On a soccer night, get to Virtue Field early, because Vermont Green FC sells out match after match and the overflow crowd fills the hill, which is free. This is the club that won the USL League Two national title in 2025 and 2026, and its supporters, the Green Mountain Bhoys among them, make their voices heard all match. On a baseball night, head to Centennial Field at 287 Colchester Avenue for the Vermont Lake Monsters. The ballpark opened in 1906 and the main grandstand went up in 1922, so pay the $5 to park, find a seat in the old grandstand and wave to Champ.

notes.vermont-green-fc: Back to back USL League Two champions, 2025 and 2026, at Virtue Field
notes.vermont-lake-monsters: Summer collegiate baseball at Centennial Field, opened in 1906

32.source: Pack the stands at a winter UVM game
32.title: Pack the stands at a winter UVM game
32.paragraph: Pick a winter weekend and check both schedules at uvmathletics.com. For hockey, head to Gutterson Fieldhouse at 97 Spear Street, the 4,007 seat rink that has hosted Catamount hockey since 1963, and settle in for a Hockey East game in one of the toughest buildings in the sport for visitors. Basketball plays at Patrick Gymnasium at the same address, where the men head into 2026-27 as the America East preseason favorite. Buy tickets ahead through the UVM ticket office online, since everyone 3 and older needs one, and park in the garage both buildings share.

notes.uvm-hockey: A 4,007 seat rink from 1963, Hockey East, first Frozen Four in 1996
notes.uvm-basketball: Patrick Gym since 1963, picked first in America East for 2026-27

33.source: Plan a weekend around a Burlington festival
33.title: Plan a weekend around a Burlington festival
33.paragraph: Circle three weekends. In early June, the Burlington Discover Jazz Festival spreads five days of music across town, with most performances free and the headline sets on the waterfront. In July, buy ahead for the Vermont Brewers Festival at Waterfront Park, where a ticket gets you tasting pours from over 40 breweries by the lake. Then, the weekend after Labor Day, walk the South End Art Hop, more than 125 locations strung along 1.5 miles of Pine Street, with thousands of pieces of art and no fee to get in.

notes.discover-jazz-festival: Five days each June, most shows free; June 2 to 6 in 2027
notes.vermont-brewers-festival: Over 40 breweries pouring at Waterfront Park each July, 21 and over
notes.south-end-art-hop: The weekend after Labor Day, 125 plus locations along Pine Street, free

34.source: Pick your own fruit from June to October
34.title: Pick your own fruit from June to October
34.paragraph: Start in June at Adam's Berry Farm in Charlotte, where certified organic strawberries come in early, raspberries follow later in June and blueberries take over in late July. In midsummer, drive south to Champlain Orchards in Shoreham for sweet and tart cherries, then peaches and plums as August goes on. Save September and October for Shelburne Orchards, where you pick apples on 60 acres near the lake, ride the hay wagon, and finish with a cider doughnut, a jug of ginger apple cider and a bottle of Dead Bird apple brandy from the tasting room.

notes.adams-berry-farm: Certified organic berries in Charlotte, strawberries from early June
notes.champlain-orchards: One of Vermont's oldest orchards, cherries to apples, 175 plus varieties
notes.shelburne-orchards: Apples on 60 acres in Sept and Oct, cider doughnuts and Dead Bird brandy

35.source: Drop down to Salmon Hole on the Winooski River
35.title: Drop down to Salmon Hole on the Winooski River
35.paragraph: Park off Riverside Avenue, just before the bridge to Winooski, and take the path down to the water. The swirling pool below the Winooski One Hydro dam is where spawning salmon gather, which is how the place got its name. Spend a while on the rocks, where the ripples and the striations in the cliff side record currents from about 500 million years ago. When you're ready to move, pick up the Riverwalk Trail and follow the Winooski River all the way to the viewing area off Intervale Road. After heavy rain, stay off flooded trails and back from the bank.

notes.salmon-hole: A 6 acre river park where salmon gather below the Winooski One dam

36.source: Eat from the food trucks on a warm evening
36.title: Eat from the food trucks on a warm evening
36.paragraph: Bike to Pine Street on a Friday, hand your bike to the Local Motion valet for free, and walk into the South End Get Down, which runs from 5 to 9 every Friday night of the summer. Check the Instagram story that morning to see which trucks are coming, then work your way down the line and grab a drink at The Pinery beer garden while the DJ plays. Dogs on a leash are welcome. When September comes, follow Park Hop Brews around South Burlington, a Thursday beer garden from 5:30 to 7:30 that lands in a different park each week with food vendors and music.

notes.south-end-get-down: Free Friday block party on Pine Street, 5 to 9, with 70 plus vendors a season
notes.park-hop-brews: A September Thursday beer garden in a new South Burlington park

37.source: Cross the river for a Winooski night out
37.title: Cross the river for a Winooski night out
37.paragraph: Book a table at Waterworks Food + Drink for 4:30 or later and ask for a seat facing the Winooski River, which is easy, since nearly every seat has the view. The room is inside the Champlain Mill, finished in 1912 as Mill No. 4 for the American Woolen Company. After dinner, cross to Main Street for a pint at Four Quarters Brewing at number 70, maybe the Space Face double IPA out in the heated biergarden. End at The Monkey House, 30 Main Street, where tickets for local bands often run $10 to $15 and a slice of pizza covers the walk home.

notes.waterworks: Dinner inside the 1912 Champlain Mill with the Winooski River outside
notes.four-quarters-brewing: Founded in 2014, now a brewery restaurant with a heated biergarden
notes.monkey-house: A small Main Street music venue, bar and pizza shop with a full calendar

38.source: Eat around the world in the Old North End
38.title: Eat around the world in the Old North End
38.paragraph: Start with tacos at Taco Gordo, each served on two fresh corn tortillas, al pastor first, with a cashew milk horchata made from scratch. Then cross to Pho Hong at 325 North Winooski Avenue, the family Vietnamese kitchen in a converted bus station, and order a bowl of pho by its number like the regulars do. Save the late slot for The Wise Fool at 260 North Street, a 25 seat room on the corner of North Winooski Avenue that serves shawarma in laffa, falafel and triple cooked fries until 11, or midnight on Friday and Saturday.

notes.taco-gordo: Cart turned restaurant, tacos on fresh corn tortillas, al pastor first
notes.pho-hong: A family Vietnamese kitchen in a converted bus station since 2008
notes.wise-fool: Shawarma in Iraqi laffa bread and triple cooked fries until late

39.source: Go on a sandwich hunt around Burlington
39.title: Go on a sandwich hunt around Burlington
39.paragraph: Bring cash and start at Four Corners of the Earth, 310 Pine Street, which opens at noon, and order the Lebanese Lamb, roasted leg of lamb grilled with aged cheddar, coleslaw and the house Sahara seasoning, toasted at the end. Expect a wait, because every one is built to order. Another day, swing by Henry Street Deli for the banh mi with coriander pork belly, pickled carrot and daikon. When you want sheer size, drive out to Martone's Market in Essex Junction and get a whole sandwich of Boar's Head meat cut to order, with a Monster Deli Pickle on the side.

notes.four-corners-of-the-earth: Cash only, the Lebanese Lamb, built to order in a Pine Street cellar
notes.henry-street-deli: A banh mi with coriander pork belly, plus waffle breakfast sandwiches
notes.martones-market: Essex Junction deli since 1992, Boar's Head sliced to order, big sandwiches

40.title: Settle Burlington's bagel argument
40.paragraph: Make it a tasting across one morning. Get to Myer's Bagels at 408 Shelburne Road when it opens at 6 and pick one up from the wood fired oven, the Montreal style that has been hand rolled here since 1997. Then head to Feldman's Bagels at 660 Pine Street for the New York side, the style Roy Feldman brought to Vermont in 1979. Finish downtown at Willow's Bagels behind City Market, open from 7:30, and pick your winner. All three close at 2, so start early.

notes.myers-bagels: Hand rolled, wood fired Montreal style since 1997 on Shelburne Road
notes.feldmans-bagels: New York style bagels and bialys, in Vermont since 1979
notes.willows-bagels: Handmade bagels boiled and baked daily behind City Market

41.source: Get a cup of Al's French Frys and a creemee
41.title: Get a cup of Al's French Frys and a creemee
41.paragraph: Pull into Al's French Frys at 1251 Williston Road and order the way folks have since 1946, a cup of frys for $3.26, or a quart for $8.94 if you're feeding the whole car, with gravy or cheese on top if the night calls for it. Add a burger if you're hungry, then finish with a Vermont creemee. The original stand had an open counter and no seats, and while the building has grown, the owners say the frys are still the same. It's open until 11, and until midnight on Friday and Saturday.

notes.als-french-fries: Fresh frys by the cup, pint or quart, plus creemees, open late nightly

42.source: Settle in for a long brunch
42.title: Settle in for a long brunch
42.paragraph: Book Juniper on Resy, which it requires if you're six or more, and settle into Hotel Vermont's lobby at 41 Cherry Street for the red flannel hash with Jericho Settlers Farm beets and Montreal-spiced brisket. Brunch runs until 1 on Saturday and Sunday, so nobody has to rush. Down by the lake, walk in to Deep City and order the Penny Cluse, eggs any style with home fries, biscuits and herb cream gravy, from the menu Charles Reeves built. Or cross the river to Sneakers Bistro in Winooski for the Kahlua French toast, and join its line online before you leave the house.

notes.juniper-hotel-vermont: Farm sourced brunch every day of the week in Hotel Vermont's lobby
notes.sneakers-bistro: A Winooski tradition since 1980, with Kahlua French toast
notes.deep-city: Penny Cluse classics by the lake, Thursday to Monday, walk in only

43.source: Pick a side in Burlington's pizza debate
43.title: Pick a side in Burlington's pizza debate
43.paragraph: Start on Saint Paul Street at Pizzeria Verità and order the Margherita, the plainest test of a Neapolitan oven, ideally on a Wednesday when it's $5 off. Then walk down Saint Paul Street to American Flatbread's Burlington Hearth for the other side of the argument and a pint of the house beer, brewed in the room where Zero Gravity got its start in 2004. For the tiebreaker, drive out to Folino's in Shelburne, where the sourdough pies come out of a 650 degree oven, and bring your own beer, since the original Folino's is BYOB and shares a building with the Fiddlehead tasting room.

notes.pizzeria-verita: Neapolitan pies from a very hot wood-fired oven, $5 off Margheritas Wednesday
notes.american-flatbread: Flatbread with beer brewed in house, where Zero Gravity began in 2004
notes.folinos: BYOB sourdough pies in a building shared with Fiddlehead in Shelburne

44.title: Drink downtown like a regular
44.paragraph: Start at the Vermont Pub & Brewery on College Street, Vermont's first brewpub, with a pint of Burly Irish Ale, and come on a Tuesday, when a Vermont or Canadian ID takes 15% off your food. Then walk over to Three Needs on Pearl Street, opened by Glenn Walter after 6 years as head brewer under Greg Noonan, and claim a pool table or a couch in the courtyard. From Tuesday through Saturday the Pizza Cube serves New Jersey boardwalk-style slices, and the bar stays open until 2 every night.

notes.vermont-pub-brewery: Vermont's first brewpub, opened in 1988, still pouring Burly Irish Ale
notes.three-needs: Pool tables, a couch courtyard and Pizza Cube slices until 2

45.source: Play unlimited pinball at the Pinball Co-op
45.title: Play unlimited pinball at the Pinball Co-op
45.paragraph: Find the white building with the 802 Fusion sign at 1881 Williston Road, head around to the back left and go through the tinted double doors. Inside, $15 buys all you can play on up to 36 machines, and since it's BYOB you can stash something in the fridge before you start. Friday is the easy night to drop in, because Wednesday is league night and league players get first pick. If you get hooked, the co-op runs leagues and a tournament every month, and nobody needs experience to sign up.

notes.pinball-coop: Up to 36 machines, $15 for unlimited play, BYOB, Wednesday and Friday nights

46.source: Climb the walls at Petra Cliffs
46.title: Climb the walls at Petra Cliffs
46.paragraph: Fill out the waiver online before you go, then walk in to Petra Cliffs at 105 Briggs Street, since there are no reservations and no time limit. Grab the $23 adult day pass and the $10 rental package, take the safety orientation, and start on the auto belays if you came alone. If you brought a friend, the $10 belay lesson gets you both onto the top rope routes, and you can leave for lunch and come back the same day. On weekdays it stays open until 10.

notes.petra-cliffs: Auto belays, top rope, lead and bouldering, with walk in lessons

47.source: Skate the waterfront park Tony Hawk endorsed
47.title: Skate the waterfront park Tony Hawk endorsed
47.paragraph: Bring your board down to the Andy A-Dog Williams Skatepark on the waterfront and warm up on the flowing street section that wraps the park before you drop into the big bowl, which runs down to 10 feet at its deep end. Take a breather on the edge and look out at the lake. The park took more than ten years of local advocacy and a Tony Hawk Foundation grant to build, and Hawk himself spun a 540 in that bowl at the 2016 naming ceremony for the late A-Dog.

notes.andy-adog-skatepark: A 21,000 square foot concrete park with a 10 foot bowl on the lake

48.source: Watch a drive-in movie or a free waterfront classic
48.title: Watch a drive-in movie or a free waterfront classic
48.paragraph: Pack the car and head to the Sunset Drive-In in Colchester, which has been putting movies on its 4 screens since 1948. Back downtown, climb to the Film House at 60 Lake Street, where Main Street Landing shows free classic films every other Tuesday at 7 on a 25 foot screen, first come, first served, so get there early and leave a donation at the door. In October, catch the Vermont International Film Festival, which started in 1985 and screens there through the year, and if you go often, a VTIFF membership gets you into its screenings free.

notes.main-street-film-house: Free classic films every other Tuesday at 7 on a 25 foot screen
notes.vtiff: Vermont's international film festival every October, plus screenings all year

49.source: Warm up downtown on a freezing night
49.title: Warm up downtown on a freezing night
49.paragraph: Start the afternoon at Lake Champlain Chocolates on Pine Street, open until 6, with a mug of the hot chocolate they bill as America's Best and a free sample. For dinner, get a bowl of tonkotsu at Gaku Ramen on Church Street, a pork broth they cook for hours, and know that it stays open late Thursday through Saturday. Then walk over to Farmhouse Tap & Grill on Bank Street and head downstairs to the Parlor, a bar built like a speakeasy, with Vermont craft beer and a fireplace worth sitting next to.

notes.lake-champlain-chocolates: America's Best hot chocolate, free samples and a $16 tasting
notes.gaku-ramen: Tonkotsu broth cooked for hours, open late Thursday through Saturday
notes.farmhouse-tap-grill: A downstairs Parlor bar with Vermont craft beer and a fireplace

50.source: Join the 3 AM slice line on Main Street
50.title: Join the 3 AM slice line on Main Street
50.paragraph: When the bars let out on a Friday or Saturday, walk down Main Street to Mr. Mike's Pizza, which keeps serving until 3, and grab a slice before you head home. Get some sleep, then come back down Main Street in the morning to Kountry Kart Deli next to the Flynn, open from 6:30, and order a Shiner at the counter that's been feeding downtown since 1989. If one sandwich won't cut it, the Hobo burger comes with a fried egg on top.

notes.mr-mikes-pizza: Main Street slices until 3 AM on Friday and Saturday nights
notes.kountry-kart-deli: Opens at 6:30 daily for Shiner breakfast sandwiches, since 1989

51.title: Do the coffee crawl
51.paragraph: Start with breakfast at August First on S. Champlain Street, which has been laptop free since 2014, so bring a friend or a book instead. Walk up to Onyx Tonics on College Street and ask which single origin coffees are on this week's menu, since it changes every week. Then head to the South End for a cup at Speeder & Earl's Pine Street café, roasting since 1993, and finish at Scout's Pine Street shop, where you can follow the coffee with a scoop of homemade ice cream.

notes.august-first: Breakfast all day in a room that's been laptop free since 2014
notes.onyx-tonics: A weekly menu of 6 or more single origin coffees
notes.speeder-and-earls: The Pine Street café of a family roastery going since 1993
notes.scout-and-company: Curated coffee and homemade ice cream in three neighborhoods

52.source: Hike a smaller mountain with a big view
52.title: Hike a smaller mountain with a big view
52.paragraph: Head past Stowe to Elmore State Park, climb the Fire Tower Trail to the 2,608 foot summit of Elmore Mountain and come down the Ridge Trail past Balancing Rock for a loop of about 4 miles, then cool off at the Lake Elmore beach. If you'd rather go south, walk the old carriage road up Snake Mountain in Addison and look across the Champlain Valley at the Adirondacks. Or stay in Stowe for the steep Stowe Pinnacle Trail to a bald summit facing Mount Mansfield, and go early on weekends, since the lot fills.

notes.elmore-state-park: A 2,608 foot summit with a fire tower and a lake beach below
notes.snake-mountain-wma: An old carriage road to views of the Champlain Valley and Adirondacks
notes.stowe-pinnacle: Short, steep and bald on top, looking straight at Mount Mansfield

53.title: Climb Ethan Allen Tower
53.paragraph: Park in the small lot off North Avenue at the Ethan Allen Parkway light, then follow the trail up through the woods to the tower Mayor William Van Patten put up in 1905. Climb to the top for a view that runs from Lake Champlain to Mt. Mansfield. Afterward, wander the dirt loops along the cliffs, or walk out to Ethan Allen Pinnacle at the north end for its gazebo and a look across the lake at Grand Isle. Come on a summer weekend, when volunteers have the tower open.

notes.ethan-allen-park: A 1905 tower over the woods with views from the lake to Mt. Mansfield

54.title: Tour Ethan Allen's homestead
54.paragraph: Get to the Ethan Allen Homestead about 30 minutes before a tour so you can watch one of the short films in the barn visitor center, then walk the 150 yards to the Allen House for the guided tour, which runs about an hour. Afterward, stroll Fanny's Garden and the recreated Abenaki village, Negôni Alnôbaakik, and save time for the riverside and wetland trails. The museum closes from November through April, but the trails stay open for hiking, snowshoeing and cross country skiing, and they connect to the Intervale's paths next door.

notes.ethan-allen-homestead: Guided tours of the 1785 Allen House, plus an Abenaki village and trails

55.title: Walk the Intervale's farm trails
55.paragraph: Park in one of the public lots off Intervale Road, stop at the information kiosk outside the Intervale Center's offices to get your bearings, and head out on the Rena Calkins Trail along the Winooski River, watching for mallards and mergansers on the water and red-tailed hawks over the fields. Keep going and the trails carry you all the way to the Ethan Allen Homestead. Come back in winter with skis or snowshoes for the 3+ miles of ungroomed cross country trails, and don't leave valuables in the car.

notes.intervale-center: 360 acres of farms and river trails, open 365 days a year

56.source: Spend an hour at the Fleming
56.title: Spend an hour at the Fleming
56.paragraph: Walk up to the Fleming Museum of Art on Colchester Avenue on a Wednesday, when it stays open until 7, and drop the suggested $5 at the welcome desk if you can. Leave your backpack in the lobby storage, since bags stay out of the galleries, and bring a pencil if you like to draw, because sketching is welcome as long as it's in pencil. Only a small share of the 25,000 works is ever out at once, and an hour is about right for what's up this term.

notes.fleming-museum: Free, with 25,000 works spanning 5,000 years and a late Wednesday

57.source: Spend a rainy hour in the Carnegie library
57.title: Spend a rainy hour in the Carnegie library
57.paragraph: Duck into the Fletcher Free Library on College Street, one block east of Church Street, the next time it rains downtown. Look up at the 1904 Carnegie building on the way in, with its windows and terracotta restored in 2026, then find a seat, pull something off the shelves and use the free internet for an hour. On a Tuesday or Wednesday it stays open until 8, and on Sunday it opens at noon.

notes.fletcher-free-library: A 1904 Carnegie building with free internet, open every day

58.title: Do the bookstore crawl
58.paragraph: Start at Phoenix Books on Church Street, browse the Vermont Authors & Illustrators shelf, and check the events calendar for a reading or open mic worth coming back for. Walk down the Marketplace to Crow Bookshop, ask what's on the current staff picks, and dig through the Old & Interesting section for something nobody else will have. Then head to the South End and give yourself real time at Speaking Volumes on Pine Street, where tens of thousands of used books share space with old magazines, ephemera and art.

notes.phoenix-books: New books, a Vermont authors section and in-store events
notes.crow-books: Thirty years on Church Street, with new, used and antiquarian shelves
notes.speaking-volumes: Tens of thousands of used and rare books, plus ephemera and art

59.title: Go on a vintage safari
59.paragraph: Check Barge Canal Market's Facebook page, then start in the South End at its Pine Street shop and work through the mid century furniture, industrial pieces and farmhouse finds. Then cross town to Junktiques Collective on N. Winooski Avenue in the Old North End, where haggling is encouraged and the shelves hold low cost goods and materials for artists. Finish at Vintage Inspired Marketplace on Dorset Street in South Burlington, open until 6, where more than 60 vendors fill the place with gifts, home decor and vintage ephemera.

notes.barge-canal-market: Mid century, industrial and farmhouse furniture on Pine Street
notes.junktiques: An Old North End reuse shop where haggling is encouraged
notes.vintage-inspired-marketplace: Over 60 antique and vintage vendors under one roof, open daily

60.title: Flip through the record stores
60.paragraph: Start downtown at Burlington Records on College Street and dig through the used bins, which live only in the shop, and ask about flattening if you own a warped favorite. Then cross the river to Autumn Records at the top of the Winooski circle, open noon to 6, where the crates cover new and used vinyl, CDs and cassettes and the shop even runs its own label. Bring a box of your old records if you're ready to part with them, since both shops buy, and Autumn takes collections from the 1950s on.

notes.burlington-records: Downtown's new and used vinyl shop, with record flattening
notes.autumn-records: Winooski's buy, sell and trade shop with its own label

61.source: Pack a local picnic and eat it by the lake
61.title: Pack a local picnic and eat it by the lake
61.paragraph: Start at City Market on South Winooski Ave, the downtown co-op where everyone is welcome to shop, member or not. Look for Miss Weinerz donuts, which the co-op carries Wednesday through Sunday, vegan sourdough made with fresh milled Vermont wheat in a New North End home bakery. Then work the aisles for the rest of the picnic, Vermont made food from over 100 local vendors, a loaf from one of more than 30 local bakeries, a sandwich from the sandwich station, or something warm off the hot bar between 11 and 7. When the bag is full, carry it down to Waterfront Park, find some grass facing the lake and spread it all out.

notes.city-market: Over 100 local vendors, open to everyone, 7 am to 9 pm every day
notes.ms-weinerz: Vegan sourdough donuts from a New North End home bakery

62.source: Watch glass get blown at AO Glass
62.title: Watch glass get blown at AO Glass
62.paragraph: Walk around behind Speeder & Earl's on Pine Street and into AO Glass, where the glassblowing is free to watch Monday through Saturday from 10 to 3, until 4 Wednesday through Friday. Stand back and watch the gaffers shape molten glass by hand, then browse the store inside the studio, stocked with glassware made right there. If watching isn't enough, book the one hour class, $175 a person for ages 16 and up, pick a bowl, vase or tumbler in your own colors, and work it start to finish with one of their glassblowers. It cools overnight in the annealing oven, so come back the next day to pick it up.

notes.ao-glass: A working hot shop you can watch for free, plus $175 make your own classes

63.source: Tour the Teddy Bear factory and Bear Hospital
63.title: Tour the Teddy Bear factory and Bear Hospital
63.paragraph: Book a tour time online for the Vermont Teddy Bear factory on Shelburne Road, $6 for adults and $2 for kids 3 to 12, since buying ahead is how you guarantee a spot. The tour starts in the Bear-racks with the company's history, then walks the assembly line, where fur is cut and stitched and heads and limbs get stuffed with recycled plastic water bottles. It ends at the Bear Hospital, where Dr. Pam admits injured bears with a form that asks about their allergies. Afterward, let the kids dream up a bear of their own in the Design Studio, or eat lunch at the picnic tables outside.

notes.vermont-teddy-bear: A factory floor tour that ends at the Bear Hospital

64.source: Taste cold climate wine and Vermont cider
64.title: Taste cold climate wine and Vermont cider
64.paragraph: Start at Shelburne Vineyard on Shelburne Road, where the vines have been in the ground since 1998, mostly cold hardy hybrids like Marquette and La Crescent that can take a Vermont winter. Order one of the two five wine flights, $18 each and waived if you buy two bottles, and pick the sweet wine and ice cider flight if dessert wine is your thing. Then drive to Stowe Cider on Town Farm Lane, open Wednesday through Sunday from noon to 9, grab a seat in the cider garden and start with High & Dry, made with no sugar at all, before working into the taproom only releases with a plate of barbecue.

notes.shelburne-vineyard: Grapes grown in Shelburne since 1998, with $18 flights daily from noon
notes.stowe-cider: Dry Vermont cider, taproom only pours and a cider garden in Stowe

65.title: Make a Vermont beer pilgrimage
65.paragraph: Start in Stowe at The Alchemist, the brewery behind Heady Topper, and order one on draft in the Beer Cafe, or book the $25 tour if you're 21 or older. Then head up Luce Hill Road to von Trapp Brewing, where the Bierhall pairs Austrian style lagers with brats, pretzels and cheddar lager soup, and the patio has big fire pits. Save Hill Farmstead in Greensboro Bend for its own day, since the taproom opens at 11:30 Wednesday through Sunday and the drive into the Northeast Kingdom is half the point. Bring a cooler, because the retail shop sells cans and bottles to take home.

notes.the-alchemist: Heady Topper on draft at the source, Beer Cafe opens at 11 daily
notes.von-trapp-bierhall: Austrian style lagers and brats in a Bierhall with fire pits
notes.hill-farmstead: Farm brewery on Hill family land, taproom Wednesday to Sunday

66.source: Eat through Waterbury, from cider donuts to barbecue
66.title: Eat through Waterbury, from cider donuts to barbecue
66.paragraph: Start early at Cold Hollow Cider Mill in Waterbury Center, open from 8 every day, where you can watch the cider press run and eat a cider donut made fresh daily. Next comes the Ben & Jerry's factory tour, 30 minutes with a MOO-vie, a look down at the production floor and a tasting in the Flavor Room, $6 for adults, and since it has sold out every day since reopening, buy tickets online, released 14 days ahead. Pay your respects at the Flavor Graveyard if it's open for the season. Then finish in Waterbury at Prohibition Pig, where the brewery around the corner from the restaurant serves lunch and dinner seven days a week.

notes.cold-hollow-cider-mill: Working cider mill since 1974 with donuts made fresh daily
notes.ben-jerrys-factory: A 30 minute tour, a Flavor Room tasting and the Flavor Graveyard
notes.prohibition-pig: Smoked meats on Main Street and a brewery open seven days a week

67.source: Taste Vermont cheese where it's made
67.title: Taste Vermont cheese where it's made
67.paragraph: Start in Stowe at Sage Farm Goat Dairy, where the self serve farm store in the buck barn sells cheese made from the farm's own Alpine goats. Look for Spruce, a creamy round wrapped in spruce bark and made in the fall, and Lightning Knoll, washed with local beers including Heady Topper, pay by card, and leave the rest of the farm to the goats. Heading south, stop at the Cabot Creamery Store in Waterbury Center, open Tuesday through Sunday from 10:30, to stock up on Cabot. Finish at Von Trapp Farmstead in Waitsfield, where the farm store is built into the barn, the cheese is organic, and the shelves carry crackers and preserves for the board.

notes.sage-farm-goat-dairy: Self serve store selling cheese from the farm's own Alpine goats
notes.cabot-creamery-store-waterbury: Cabot's own Creamery Store, open Tuesday through Sunday
notes.von-trapp-farmstead: Organic farmstead cheese from a farm store built into the barn

68.title: Sip spirits distilled in Vermont
68.paragraph: Start downtown at Mad River Distillers on St. Paul Street, where a tasting flight walks you through whiskey, rum and apple brandy made in Warren, then stay for a cocktail. Walk over to the Smugglers' Notch Distillery tasting room at 28 Church Street, open daily 11 to 7, to try its small batch spirits. For the full trip, drive to Montpelier and Barr Hill on Gin Lane, the only place its gin and vodka are distilled. Take the free 15 minute tour of the distillery floor, barrel room and bottling line, then settle in at the bar, where weekend lunch runs until 3:30.

notes.mad-river-distillers: Warren whiskey, rum and brandy in flights and cocktails downtown
notes.smugglers-notch-distillery: A Church Street tasting room open daily 11 to 7
notes.barr-hill-distillery: Free tours and a James Beard nominated bar where the gin is made

69.source: Cool off in a Vermont swimming hole
69.title: Cool off in a Vermont swimming hole
69.paragraph: For the classic, head to Warren Falls on Route 100, park in the lot on the west side of the highway, never on the road itself, and follow the short paths down to the deep pools of the Mad River below the cliffs. Pack out everything you bring and leave the rocks where they are, since rock dams hurt the river life. Bartlett Falls in Bristol is the one where swimmers swim up into the cave behind the falling water, so park well off Lincoln Road. In Johnson, Journey's End on Foote Brook is quieter, a half mile of stream the town owns and protects, with a small pull-off on Plot Road and dogs welcome on leash.

notes.warren-falls: Deep Mad River pools on national forest land, with a real parking lot
notes.bristol-falls: Swim up into the cave behind a 15 foot waterfall
notes.journeys-end-swimming-hole: A town owned half mile of Foote Brook, quieter and dog friendly

70.source: Take a short walk to a waterfall
70.title: Take a short walk to a waterfall
70.paragraph: Pick one, or chain two in a day. In Stowe, Moss Glen Falls is the easy win, a quarter mile walk with bog bridging over the wet spots to a 125 foot cascade. Bingham Falls, off Route 108, is a quarter mile down a steep path that gets slippery near the bottom, so wear real shoes and keep kids well back from the roped gorge edges. Farther south in Hancock, Texas Falls has a 1 mile loop past viewpoints and a bridge over the falls, where you can see the potholes glacial meltwater carved into the rock. Leave the swimsuit home, since swimming isn't allowed there.

notes.moss-glen-falls: A 125 foot cascade a quarter mile from the car
notes.bingham-falls: A steep quarter mile down to a gorge in Smugglers' Notch State Park
notes.texas-falls: Glacial potholes and a bridge over the falls on a 1 mile loop

71.source: Float the Winooski in a tube
71.title: Float the Winooski in a tube
71.paragraph: Pick a hot day, Thursday through Saturday, and book the Richmond float with Umiak, $35 a person for the tube and the shuttle. Meet at Overocker Park on Cochran Road, wear clothes and closed toe shoes you don't mind soaking, and the driver takes you upriver with a few safety tips on the way. Then it's 2.5 lazy miles of Winooski River back to the car, about 2 to 3 hours depending on the water. Add the $9 Tube and Brew voucher and finish with a tasting flight at Stone Corral, or add $5 for a creemee instead. Kids need to be at least 6.

notes.umiak-tubing: Tube and shuttle included, with a beer or creemee add on

72.title: Paddle out onto Lake Champlain
72.paragraph: Walk down to the Community Sailing Center on the waterfront, grab a kayak, canoe or paddleboard at $16 an hour, and head along the breakwater or out toward North Beach, keeping it to the two hour max. If you'd rather launch off a beach, the Burlington Surf Club on Lakeside Ave rents paddleboards by the hour, with foil boards and windsurfers for the ambitious. And if paddling alone sounds lonely, watch for one of Mālia's free try it sessions, when the dragon boat team that has called the sailing center home since 2013 takes newcomers out on the lake.

notes.community-sailing-center: Kayaks, canoes and boards for $16 an hour, first come first served
notes.burlington-surf-club: Paddleboards, foil boards and windsurfers off a South End beach
notes.malia-dragon-boating: Free try it sessions with the dragon boat team each summer

73.source: Sweat it out in a lakeside sauna or a spa
73.title: Sweat it out in a lakeside sauna or a spa
73.paragraph: Book a private session at Savu Lakeside, 50 Lakeside Ave, where two outdoor saunas look out on the lake and robes and towels are waiting. Work the cycle the way they suggest, sweat, plunge into cold water, rest, and repeat. If you'd rather sweat with neighbors, the Hula Happy Hour runs Tuesday and Wednesday evenings from 5:30 to 6:30, $20 a person, bring your own towel and water bottle, and the cold plunge is the lake itself. For a slower day, the Essex Resort & Spa books massages and facials and has an indoor lap pool and an outdoor pool for in between.

notes.savu-sauna: Private lakeside saunas by the hour, or a $20 community session
notes.essex-resort-spa: Massages, facials and pools for a full spa day in Essex

74.source: Take small kids swimming at Sand Bar
74.title: Take small kids swimming at Sand Bar
74.paragraph: Pack the sunscreen and the sand toys and drive up U.S. Route 2 to Sand Bar State Park in Milton, open from Memorial Day weekend through Labor Day weekend, 10 to sunset. Day use is $5 for anyone 14 and up and $2 for kids 4 to 13. The draw is the bottom, smooth sand that stays shallow well out from the 2,000 foot beach, so little ones can wade into Lake Champlain without the water getting deep fast. Set up near the play area and the grills, rent a kayak if the grown ups get restless, and leave the dog at home, since pets aren't allowed.

notes.sandbar-state-park: Shallow, sandy water well out from shore, popular with families

75.source: Find a quiet trail close to town
75.title: Find a quiet trail close to town
75.paragraph: Go early and pick by mood. Centennial Woods is the one you can reach on foot from UVM, 70 acres of conifers, streams and wetland with free parking on weekends. Colchester Pond rewards a longer outing, a 3.5 mile loop around a mile long pond where beavers visit and bobcat and moose have left their signs. Niquette Bay State Park climbs two ridges to views of Malletts Bay, then drops to Lake Champlain for a swim in season. Out in Huntington, the Green Mountain Audubon Center has five miles of trail through hemlock swamp and along the Huntington River, with boardwalks at Peeper Pond and binoculars to borrow.

notes.centennial-woods: UVM's 70 acre woods, reachable on foot from campus
notes.colchester-pond: A 3.5 mile loop around a mile long pond with moose and bobcat signs
notes.niquette-bay-state-park: Two ridges with Malletts Bay views, then a beach
notes.audubon-vermont: Five miles of trail, boardwalks at Peeper Pond, binoculars to borrow

76.title: Ride Vermont's mountain bike trails
76.paragraph: Warm up close to home at Sunny Hollow in Colchester, where the Blueberry and East loops are made for beginners, then try Saxon Hill in Essex, where Flo has loops for every level and FreeFall is a jump trail for advanced riders. When you're ready for a road trip, Millstone Trails rides through historic quarries and regrowing forest around the Barre Town Forest, $10 for a day pass. Save a full weekend for Kingdom Trails in East Burke, 100+ miles of trail that exist because more than 100 landowners let riders cross their land, so buy your membership, stay on the trail and say thanks.

notes.sunny-hollow: Beginner loops in Colchester, kept up by the Fellowship of the Wheel
notes.saxon-hill: Classic smooth, flowy singletrack in Essex, from Extendo to FreeFall
notes.millstone-trails: Singletrack through historic quarries for a $10 day pass
notes.kingdom-trails: A 100+ mile network on the land of more than 100 landowners

77.source: Spend a summer day out on the Champlain Islands
77.title: Spend a summer day out on the Champlain Islands
77.paragraph: Take I-89 Exit 17 and let Route 2 carry you through South Hero, Grand Isle and North Hero. Pull into Knight Point State Park for a swim off the beach and the easy trail that loops around the point, past the rebuilt Knight Tavern from 1790. Then follow Route 129 onto Isle La Motte. Saint Anne's Shrine sits right on the water where the French put up a fort and chapel in 1666, with rustic grottos, picnic spots, and snacks and ice cream served daily. Finish at the Goodsell Ridge Fossil Preserve, where a free self guided tour shows you fossils from the Chazy Fossil Reef.

notes.knight-point-state-park: A summer swimming beach and a loop trail around the point on North Hero
notes.st-annes-shrine: The lakeside shrine on the site of the 1666 French fort and chapel
notes.goodsell-ridge-fossil-preserve: Free and open dawn to dusk, a walk across the Chazy Fossil Reef

78.source: Spend a day in Montpelier, the smallest capital
78.title: Spend a day in Montpelier, the smallest capital
78.paragraph: Start at the Vermont State House on State Street. Grab a free audio tour wand, or join a free guided tour from July through October, and take in the House and Senate chambers, the oldest active legislative halls in the country that still have their original interiors. Come between January and May and you can watch the session as space allows. Walk next door to the Vermont History Museum in the Pavilion Building, $9 for adults, open Tuesday through Saturday. Then head to Hunger Mountain Co-op for a soup and sandwich from the deli and cafe.

notes.vermont-state-house: Free tours and the oldest legislative chambers with original interiors
notes.vermont-history-museum: The state's story in the Pavilion Building, right next to the State House
notes.hunger-mountain-coop: A member owned co-op whose deli and cafe make the lunch stop

79.source: Spend a day in Middlebury and meet the Morgans
79.title: Spend a day in Middlebury and meet the Morgans
79.paragraph: Drive down to Weybridge first for the UVM Morgan Horse Farm, where more than 40 Morgans live on the farm Colonel Joseph Battell founded in 1878. Pay the $10 adult admission in the gift shop in the main barn, then take a guided tour or wander on your own. Head into Middlebury for lunch at Otter Creek Bakery on College Street, a European style bakery and deli baking since 1986, and finish at the Middlebury College Museum of Art, where admission is free and the galleries are open Tuesday through Sunday.

notes.uvm-morgan-horse-farm: More than 40 Morgans on Colonel Battell's 1878 farm, open May to October
notes.otter-creek-bakery: A European style bakery and deli on College Street since 1986
notes.middlebury-college-museum-of-art: Free admission to the college's art collection, Tuesday through Sunday

80.title: Ski the independent hills
80.paragraph: Start close to home at Cochran's Ski Area in Richmond, the nonprofit hill that grew from Mickey and Ginny Cochran's 1961 backyard rope tow. It's the home hill of Barbara Ann Cochran, 1972 Olympic gold, and her son Ryan Cochran-Siegle, who won Olympic silver in 2022 and again in 2026. On a weeknight, drive up to Bolton Valley, Vermont's only night skiing, and ride until 10 on a night ticket from $29. Save a powder day for Mad River Glen in Fayston, the skier owned co-op where snowboards are banned and the 1948 Single Chair still carries you up one at a time.

notes.cochrans-ski-area: The nonprofit family hill behind Olympic medals in 1972, 2022 and 2026
notes.bolton-valley: Vermont's only night skiing, typically Tuesday to Saturday until 10
notes.mad-river-glen: Skier owned, no snowboards, and the 1948 Single Chair

81.source: Cross-country ski out to a cabin in the woods
81.title: Cross-country ski out to a cabin in the woods
81.paragraph: Drive to Stowe, pick up rentals at the von Trapp Outdoor Center and ski out to the Slayton Pasture Cabin, where homemade soup, sandwiches and hot chocolate wait by a roaring fireplace. A 2026-27 adult pass is $33 on weekdays and $37 on weekends. Closer to home, Sleepy Hollow in Huntington grooms 32 kilometers and stays open for night skiing on weeknights, and the trail to Butternut Cabin, about a mile out, ends on a porch facing Camel's Hump. For a shorter outing, Catamount in Williston grooms over 35 kilometers, and snowshoeing there is free.

notes.von-trapp-nordic: The country's first cross-country ski center, with soup by the cabin fire
notes.sleepy-hollow-nordic: Weeknight night skiing and a cabin porch facing Camel's Hump
notes.catamount-outdoor-center: Over 35 kilometers in Williston, and snowshoeing is free

82.source: Go public skating at a local rink
82.title: Go public skating at a local rink
82.paragraph: Lace up at Leddy Park, where the city's Gordon H. Paquette Ice Arena holds public skate sessions on weekday mornings and Sunday afternoons. Admission is $5 for adults, $4 for children and students and free for anyone 65 and up, and if you don't own skates, rentals are $5 a pair at the rink. Check the city's recreation calendar for the week's sessions before you go. If Leddy's times don't fit, the C. Douglas Cairns Recreation Arena on Swift Street in South Burlington runs its own public skating schedule, posted on the arena's site.

notes.leddy-arena: The city rink at Leddy Park, $5 public skates and $5 rentals
notes.cairns-arena: South Burlington's arena on Swift Street, with its own public skates

83.source: Try ice fishing on Vermont's free day
83.title: Try ice fishing on Vermont's free day
83.paragraph: Mark the last Saturday in January, Vermont's Free Ice Fishing Day, when anyone can drop a line through the ice on any water open to ice fishing without a license. Head to the free Ice Fishing Festival, which Vermont Fish and Wildlife moves around the state each winter, and let staff and Let's Go Fishing instructors walk you through knots, baiting and tip-ups, with gear on loan and a fish fry cooking up the catch. Wear ice cleats and warm layers, go with a friend, and look for at least three to four inches of clear black ice.

notes.free-ice-fishing-day: One Saturday a year with no license needed, gear loaned and lessons on the ice

84.source: Skate across a frozen pond into the sea cave
84.title: Skate across a frozen pond into the sea cave
84.paragraph: Wait for a long stretch of hard cold, then park in the Burlington High School lot and cross North Avenue to the Winooski Valley Park District trail. It's about a five minute walk down to the pond, then roughly 600 feet along the edge, on skates or boots, to the cave, one big chamber of orange dolostone. Vermont Fish and Wildlife says three to four inches of clear black ice is the minimum to walk on, and ice near inlets and pressure cracks can be thinner, so test it as you go, bring a friend, and turn back if you're unsure.

notes.donahue-sea-caves: A pond cave you can only skate or walk into once the ice is thick

85.source: Jump in the lake for the Penguin Plunge
85.title: Jump in the lake for the Penguin Plunge
85.paragraph: Sign up on the Penguin Plunge site as a solo plunger or with a team, then spend the next few weeks hitting up friends for donations, since every plunger commits to raising at least $250. On Saturday, February 6, 2027, head to the Burlington Waterfront for an 11 start and run into Lake Champlain with everybody else. The 2026 plunge, the 31st, drew over 1,100 people and raised over $585,000 for Special Olympics Vermont, money that lets athletes take part in sports and competitions at no cost. Plungers under 18 need a parent or guardian to sign the waiver.

notes.penguin-plunge: Special Olympics Vermont's biggest fundraiser, straight into the lake

86.source: Walk out to where the Winooski meets the lake
86.title: Walk out to where the Winooski meets the lake
86.paragraph: Ride in on the Island Line and cross the bike bridge over the mouth of the Winooski River from Mayes Landing, or take one of the few spots in the small lot off Windemere Way in Colchester. Follow the half mile elevated path through floodplain forest and marsh, with the lake and the Adirondacks opening up ahead, and bring binoculars, since Audubon Vermont counts Delta Park among the 17 Important Bird Areas in the state. Then walk out onto the sandy beach, a rare thing on this shore, and give the turtle nesting areas plenty of room.

notes.delta-park: A raised path to the river mouth and rare natural sandy lakeshore

87.source: Drive Smugglers' Notch before winter closes it
87.title: Drive Smugglers' Notch before winter closes it
87.paragraph: Go in summer or fall, since the state closes Route 108 through the Notch in winter. Start at the Barnes Camp Visitor Center and walk the wetlands boardwalk, then drive the 3.5 mile stretch as it winds up between cliffs nearly 1,000 feet tall, past boulders that still catch trucks every year. Pull over at the Smugglers' Notch Picnic Area beside the stream and picture the folks who herded cattle to Canada after the 1807 Embargo Act, and the liquor runners of the 1920s. If your legs are fresh, the Sterling Pond Trail starts up here too.

notes.smugglers-notch-drive: Route 108's narrow pass under cliffs nearly 1,000 feet tall, closed in winter

88.source: Ride the dinner train down the Champlain Valley
88.title: Ride the dinner train down the Champlain Valley
88.paragraph: Check in inside the Burlington Amtrak station at 1 Main Street, since every train boards from that platform, and settle in at your table for the three hour round trip to Middlebury and back. The three course dinner is made on board in the kitchen car, you pick your entree once you're rolling, and gratuity is already included, so the only extra is whatever you order from the full bar. The cars are climate controlled, with restrooms aboard. Trains run weekend evenings in summer and Friday through Sunday into late October, so book ahead.

notes.champlain-valley-dinner-train: Three courses cooked aboard, boarding at Burlington's Amtrak station

89.source: Take a ghost walk through Burlington's dark side
89.title: Take a ghost walk through Burlington's dark side
89.paragraph: Buy tickets ahead, since many walks sell out, and get there 15 minutes early. The classic pick is Darkness Falls, which meets at the Democracy Sculpture on Courthouse Plaza at 199 Main Street and covers theater ghosts, smugglers and serial killers, best for ten and up. For something stranger, Fright by Flashlight takes you into Lakeview Cemetery with vintage ghost hunting tools, and Ghosts and Legends of Lake Champlain digs into the waterfront's scandalous past from Union Station. Thea Lewis, who started the tours in 2002, writes every story you'll hear.

notes.queen-city-ghost-walk: Burlington's original ghost tour, written by the historian who leads it

90.source: Hunt down the small, specific museums
90.title: Hunt down the small, specific museums
90.paragraph: Make a summer loop of it, starting in Jericho at the Old Red Mill, where the free Snowflake Bentley Exhibit shows the farmer's original snow crystal photographs and his camera. Head south to Ferrisburgh for Rokeby Museum and its Underground Railroad story, told through four generations of the Robinson family, and walk its trails, open year round. Finish on the water at the Lake Champlain Maritime Museum in Vergennes, free and open daily from May to October. Save the Hyde Log Cabin in Grand Isle, built in 1783, for a day out on the islands.

notes.snowflake-bentley-exhibit: Free, with Bentley's original snow crystal photos and camera
notes.rokeby-museum: A nationally significant Underground Railroad story on a family farm
notes.lc-maritime-museum: Always free, open daily May to October on Basin Harbor Road
notes.hyde-log-cabin: A 1783 log cabin in Grand Isle, open late May to Columbus Day

91.source: See professional theater at Vermont Stage
91.title: See professional theater at Vermont Stage
91.paragraph: Pick a show from Vermont Stage's season and head to 60 Lake Street, third floor, where Burlington's professional theater company has been working since 1994 and has staged more than 200 productions. Start with Winter Tales in December, when Patti Casey and friends come back with funny and heartfelt stories and songs for the dark days, then return for a play in the new year, since the 2026-27 season runs through May 23, 2027. Call the box office Tuesday through Friday, noon to 5, to grab seats.

notes.vermont-stage: Professional theatre with more than 200 productions since 1994

92.title: Collect the area's quirkiest landmarks
92.paragraph: Start in the South End at 208 Flynn Avenue, where the World's Tallest Filing Cabinet, 38 rusting drawers by Bren Alvarez, stands on its 10 foot pedestal, each drawer counting a year the Southern Connector went unbuilt. Then get on I-89 and watch for Jim Sardonis's black granite whale tails, Reverence, diving into the grass in South Burlington, where they've surfaced since 1999. Finish in Richmond at the Round Church, a sixteen sided meeting house raised in 1812 and 1813, where Richmond Historical Society volunteers guide visitors in summer and early fall.

notes.worlds-tallest-filing-cabinet: 38 drawers, one for every year the Southern Connector went unbuilt
notes.whale-tails-sculpture: Sardonis's granite tails diving into the grass beside I-89
notes.old-round-church: A sixteen sided meeting house from 1812 and 1813, a National Historic Landmark

93.source: Fix, borrow, or make something instead of buying it
93.title: Fix, borrow, or make something instead of buying it
93.paragraph: Start on Pine Street at The Makery, number 388, a secondhand art and craft supply store that also hosts a free Bring Your Own Craft Night once a month, no registration needed. Further down Pine at 688, Sandbox repairs clothing, backpacks and technical outerwear, and swaps out busted zippers. Then cross town to Old Spokes Home on North Winooski Avenue, where used bikes and parts are the specialty and flat fixes start at $15. Finish in South Burlington, where the library's Library of Things lends games, tools and even a telescope to cardholders 16 and up, nonresidents included.

notes.the-makery: Secondhand craft supplies and a free monthly craft night, no signup
notes.sandbox-repair: Clothing, pack and outerwear repair, with busted zippers swapped
notes.old-spokes-home: Used bikes and parts, with flat fixes from $15
notes.south-burlington-library: A Library of Things lending games, tools and even a telescope

94.source: Learn to contra dance on a Friday night
94.title: Learn to contra dance on a Friday night
94.paragraph: Queen City Contras has kept contra dancing, an old New England tradition, going around Burlington for over thirty years.
